newsitem.title: USA: Surging dlr comfortably over 1.80 marks at US noon.
newsitem.headline: Surging dlr comfortably over 1.80 marks at US noon.

text.p: A surging dollar stood comfortably above the 1.80 mark level at midday after surging to another near-six year peak against the German currency with the help of a rejuvenated dollar/yen.

The greenback retreated after its initial morning blip above 1.80 marks, but reclaimed the key psychological level as fears of profit-taking and central bank intervention eased somewhat, dealers said.
"Dollar/mark failed up here a few times and when dollar/yen took off people felt more comfortable buying it," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suisse First Boston.

At midday, the dollar stood 1.8026/31 marks, well above its opening level of 1.7940/45 and an overseas session low of 1.7830. Its peak for the day was 1.8040 marks -- the rate's highest level since August of 1991.

Dollar/yen, which had been stuck in an extremely tight range in recent weeks, was up almost two-yen from Monday's close, helped by a recovery in the mark/yen cross and reports that large investors were buying yen put options.
"The yen probably has more legs than dollar/mark at this juncture," said a trader at a U.S. bank. "If we do get a close above 115 that will be considered very positive."
Dollar/yen was changing hands at 115.77/82 at midday, up from 114.38/43 at the open and 113.95/05 at the close of trade on Monday.

The impetus for dollar/yen's move came from senior Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, who was quoted in wire reports as saying the foreign exchange market had excessive and unjustified expectations for the yen's appreciation, and that G7 nations had no intention of using currency rates as a trade tool.
But the main story on Tuesday was dollar/mark, which showed no signs of ending its momentous climb.

Comments from German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who accused foreign exchange markets of overreacting in sending the pound and dollar to recent multi-year highs against the mark, did knock dollar/mark back in overseas dealings.
But during U.S. time, dealers took the weakness as an opportunity to buy into the long dollar/mark trade, pushing it above the much anticipated 1.80 level.

"Many investors and traders felt that they'd missed the move and took advantage of the pullback in the dollar to buy again," said John Rothfield, interenational economist at NationsBanc-CRT in Chicago.
Technicians pegged the next objective in dollar/mark at 1.8075 and said a stretch to the 1.85 level was now very much in the cards.

Market observers were also turning increasingly bullish on dollar/yen, targeting the 117.10/20 level over the near-term. They said that Japanese exporters, which were rumored to have offers around 114.75/85 earlier, likely pulled those orders and rode the rate higher.
Dealers were encouraged that Tuesday's dollar move against the mark and yen appeared less dependent on cross rates.

Nevertheless, the mark remained under pressure against European currencies. Dealers reported for the second consecutive day that the Bank of Italy was buying marks for lire to stem strength in its currency.
Mark/lira stood at 971.40/70 in the early afternoon, above its session low of 970.70.
In other trade, the dollar pushed up to 1.4792/02 Swiss francs against 1.4717/22 at the open, and climbed to Canadian $1.3703/08 from C$1.3670/75.
Sterling, which stood near the middle of the day's range above 3.0 marks, was weaker at $1.6760/70 versus $1.6848/55.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
